summary:
The Komi Republic stands under the legal framework of Russia, which applies in full. The sources identify no variation in how these laws operate at the level of the republic, and the jurisdiction is assessed at the national position. A trans visitor to Syktyvkar or anywhere else in the Komi Republic faces the same legal exposure as a trans visitor elsewhere in Russia.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; gender-marker changes on documents remain prohibited, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year, and same-sex marriage is barred. Same-sex sexual activity itself is not criminalised.

The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising six to ten years. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 of them administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Trans-specific physical coercion is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman, lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department's travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement; the advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. The same note treats Chechnya, an autonomous republic within Russia, as part of the country-wide pattern rather than an isolated case.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Komi Republic live under the same prohibition on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care that applies across Russia, so a person already resident in Syktyvkar has no domestic route to change a marker on internal documents or to obtain trans-specific medical treatment through official channels.

Russian nationals face the administrative and criminal penalties attached to the propaganda statutes and to the extremist designation, including the two-to-six-year and six-to-six-year ranges for participation and organising, without the deportation option available to foreign nationals. The UK Home Office's finding that the Russian state is able but unwilling to protect LGBT+ people bears directly on domestic protection mechanisms rather than on entry decisions.

No source in the inventory identifies a republic-level body, programme or police practice in the Komi Republic that diverges from the national position in either direction, and none records local support services, shelters or transition-care providers operating legally within the republic.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether passport or identity-document screening at Russian border points singles out documents with inconsistent gender markers is not addressed in the sources; the entry-risk assessment rests on the general travel advisory and on the stated penalties for foreigners rather than on documented screening practice.

Hate-crime enhancement for offences motivated by gender identity, and whether any such charges have been brought in the Komi Republic, is not sourced here. The inventory contains no Komi-specific incident data, court records or police-reporting figures for the republic.

The reach of the banned-symbol provisions into ordinary clothing, jewellery or online profiles is described only through the national administrative case count; how article 20.3 is applied in this republic specifically remains unresolved in these sources.
